- If sentiment is positive (≥ 0.67) in recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast slope or cap upward momentum.
- If sentiment is negative (≤ 0.33) or volatile, model often underestimates downside risk; add buffer for sharp drops or adjust downward bias.
- After a sharp price spike (e.g., >10% from prior peak), model frequently overshoots and fails to correct; apply “cool-down” rule: reduce forecast by 5–10% for next 3–5 periods.
- Model exhibits strong mean reversion bias: if price is trending sharply upward, forecast often continues upward too long; apply “reversion ceiling” — cap forecast at 1.5x recent high if sentiment is neutral or negative.
- When sentiment is flat (0.00–0.33) and price is trending, model often fails to capture mean reversion; add “trend decay” rule: reduce forecast slope by 10–20% if no sentiment signal.
- For 30-day horizon, model consistently overestimates early periods (first 5–7 days) after spikes; apply “early lag correction”: reduce first 5 forecast points by 2–5% if sentiment was positive.
- If sentiment history shows repeated 0.67–1.00 spikes, model tends to overreact; apply “sentiment saturation” rule: cap forecast growth rate at 0.5% per day after 3 consecutive high sentiment days.
